input.lead: Women with endometriosis are suffering financially as well as physically, a new report by MPs warns
input.summary: Women with endometriosis are suffering financially as well as physically, a new report by MPs warns
input.evidence_text: 'Some think endometriosis is just a bad period, but it's so much worse' - BBC News Image source, Megan Gomersall Image caption, Megan Gomersall has been out of work for about two and a half years because of her symptoms By James Fell and Mat Trewern , North West Published 15 October 2026 Women with endometriosis are being forced out of work, losing income and facing significant financial hardship because of the condition, according to a new report by MPs. The inquiry by the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Endometriosis, supported by Endometriosis UK, found 47% of women with the condition had lost income because of their symptoms, while 28% had left a job altogether. Among them was Chloe Ward, from Bolton, who said her endometriosis - which can cause severe pain, fatigue, heavy bleeding and fertility problems - had cost her thousands of pounds and affected her ability to run her own business. She said: "A lot of people think it's just a bad period, but it's so much worse." Image source, Chloe Ward Image caption, Chloe Ward says years of treatment, surgery and time off work have left her paying a heavy financial price for endometriosis About one in 10 women suffer from the condition, but diagnosis can be a lengthy process. Chloe said it took seven years for her to be diagnosed. She said being self-employed in the beauty industry meant she had flexibility, but no financial safety net. "If I'm not there to do the treatments, nobody pays me," she said. She told BBC Radio Manchester she had lost clients over the years because flare-ups could leave her unable to work at short notice. Chloe is now waiting for a hysterectomy, which will mean more time away from work. "There's so much to it that people don't understand," she said. The financial impact has extended beyond lost ea

input.evidence_text: Police appeal after £10,000 air conditioning units stolen from Altrincham opticians Skip to content News — Police, Fire & Court Police appeal after £10,000 air conditioning units stolen from Altrincham opticians Police have released an image of the two men they wish to speak to. , and David Prior October 15, 2026 . 5:42 PM 1 min read Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Share via Email Police are appealing for information after two air conditioning units worth a total of £10,000 were stolen from an opticians in Altrincham town centre. The units were taken from Maskell + Josephson opticians on Regent Road in the early hours of Tuesday 6 October. Greater Manchester Police said two men were seen entering a courtyard behind the business carrying cutters between 11.10am and 11.20am on Monday 5 October. The men subsequently left the courtyard, after which the air conditioning units reportedly fell from the wall. The two men police want to speak to Police believe the same two men returned to the courtyard at around 6am the following morning and removed the two units. Officers have released images of two men they would like to speak to in connection with the theft, as they believe they could assist with their enquiries. Anyone with information is asked to contact GMP on 101 or via LiveChat, quoting crime reference CRI/06MM/0015143/26. What better way to avoid those endless queues, chaotic traffic and stressful homeward journeys? Clock off and skip the rush-hour traffic while you watch live jazz and make the most of our happy hour deals from 5–7pm: £4.50 pints / 2 for £15 cocktails / £15 bottles of wine + pizzas from £5! title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round

input.evidence_text: In 1965, The Sunday Times Magazine sent photojournalist John Bulmer north to document the region at a time when it was defined by industrial decline. But the images he returned with told a more complex story: shot in colour, they showed humanity and dignity alongside the hardship Sixty years later, photographer Simon Hill has retraced that journey. The conversation between their two bodies of work, now showing together at Jodrell Bank, builds a portrait of how much has changed since then and how much remains While Bulmer visited 16 locations across the North, Hill travelled to more than 50. From late 2024 to mid 2026 he crossed the historic seven counties from Newcastle to Liverpool, visiting former mining communities, coastal towns, city centres, remote landscapes, and the motorways In homage to Bulmer’s pioneering use of colour, much of Hill’s work was shot on Harman Phoenix 200, a contemporary colour film made in the North, and known for its unpredictable, textured qualities Bulmer’s North captured communities facing uncertain futures as the industries that defined them began to disappear. Hill’s is post-industrial, more diverse and still evolving. Former centres of heavy industry have become sites of cultural reinvention and technological growth. input.evidence_text: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and thousands of bargain hunters each week. Sellers can arrive and set up from 6:00 AM, with buyers welcomed in from 7:00 AM. Entry costs just £1 per car for buyers. Pitches for sellers are £14 for a car, £20 for a van and £3 for a trailer, with regular and corner pitches available on request. Bring exact change to keep the queue moving, and call organiser Andrew on 07470784644 for more details. Expect hundreds of stalls across the concrete hardstanding pitches, so it goes ahead in most weather. On-site you'll find a 5-star catering service, doughnuts and coffee, ice cream and desserts, a meat auction, fresh fruit and veg, plants, and retro sweet stalls. The sale is dog-friendly, has male and female toilets, ample parking, and kids' rides and bouncy castles to keep little ones entertained.
